episode_title: Advantaged Podcast, S2E20: Inside SAP.iO's Fund, Foundries, and Venture Studio (with Ram Jambunathan)

real_qa.q: What was the core insight behind SAP.iO's proposal to the SAP board in 2015?
real_qa.r: The core insight was based on the innovators dilemma—SAP was listening to its largest, most profitable customers and following their roadmaps instead of taking bets on where the next wave of technology was heading. SAP had missed shifts in cloud, mobile, and other technology areas, and wanted to create a sensing mechanism to the next wave of innovation, particularly around machine learning, while also stimulating an ecosystem around their HANA in-memory database platform.

real_qa.q: What three critical elements did Ram Jambunathan identify as necessary for SAP.iO to succeed?
real_qa.r: He stressed three things: executive mandate (board and CEO level initiative so people take it seriously and appropriate resources), creative structure (creating an avenue to think differently, including process changes and even physical spaces like the San Francisco office that did not look like SAP), and patient capital (protecting funding from quarterly business ebbs and flows since startup journeys are multi-year bets).
real_qa.requete: SAP.iO three elements executive mandate creative structure patient capital

real_qa.q: How did SAP structure the initial funding for SAP.iO and what was the capital allocation?
real_qa.r: SAP set up a $35 million fund to invest in external startups, with additional OPEX to drive internal activities including their foundries and venture studio. The funding was meant to be testable—testing hypotheses and reacting accordingly rather than instantiating a huge sum all at once.
real_qa.requete: $35 million SAP.iO fund external startups foundries

real_qa.q: What was Ram Jambunathan's experience as a founder in the fiber optics and semiconductor space?
real_qa.r: In 2000, he left Bell Labs with colleagues to start a fiber optics company backed by Sequoia, Greylock, and U.S. Venture Partners, raising $16 million in Series A funding. They built a semiconductor fab and packaging line from scratch in Allentown, Pennsylvania, competing with companies 100 times their size like Fujitsu, Sumitomo, and Lucent. The company survived the dot-com crash by demonstrating better quality products as competitors retrenched, and was ultimately acquired with the technology becoming part of Broadcom.
real_qa.requete: Ram Jambunathan fiber optics startup Allentown Broadcom acquisition

real_qa.q: How did SAP maintain board and executive support for SAP.iO's patient capital approach beyond initial approval?
real_qa.r: Ram emphasized that you need to keep selling the value continuously. SAP gave quarterly updates to the top 400-500 executives at the company, ensured the executive and supervisory boards were abreast of delivered value, and had internal startups present at supervisory board meetings. They also built internal marketing initiatives and branding efforts, including maintaining a separate sap.io website rather than being buried under sap.com, to communicate the initiative's value across all levels.
real_qa.requete: SAP.iO patient capital governance quarterly executive updates

guest.bio_context: Ram spent 15 years at SAP, ultimately as General Manager running SAP.iO, which was SAP's investment and incubation arm that he helped launch in 2015. Before SAP, he was a co-founder of a fiber optics company backed by Sequoia, Greylock, and U.S. Venture Partners, and worked at Bell Labs on high-speed optical telecommunications. He also studied for a PhD in Optoelectronics at the University of Michigan and worked as a management consultant at McKinsey.
